scores.evidence: CRDT (Yjs or Automerge): Recommended. It supports offline editing and peer-to-peer setups, and mature libraries exist.
scores.rationale: Technical claims about CRDTs, OT/ShareDB needing central ordering, y-prosemirror, Hocuspocus, IndexedDB and Redis pub/sub are all accurate; it just never reaches subtle areas like CRDT metadata overhead or rich-text intent limits.

scores.evidence: I'm reading "order" as putting the build steps in sequence. Each phase below depends on the ones before it
scores.rationale: Resolves the ambiguous request sensibly, covers the core capabilities (merge, sync, persistence, presence, permissions, offline) with a credibly buildable sequence; gaps like collaborative undo and protocol versioning are minor.

scores.evidence: Connect the editor's state to the CRDT document (for example, `y-prosemirror`).
scores.rationale: The Phase 0 CRDT decision is honored consistently through storage, offline cache, and single-server-per-document routing; the Phase 1 REST save path that later becomes CRDT update storage is a trivial loose end, not a contradiction.

scores.evidence: confirm all copies end up the same. This is the riskiest part of the project, so test it early.
scores.rationale: The riskiest assumption (convergence) is tested early, every phase ends in a checkable milestone, and drift alerts plus load testing continue validation post-launch, though test rigor (reordered/duplicated delivery) and acceptance criteria are thin.

scores.evidence: Set your targets: how many people can edit one document at once, acceptable delay (aim for under 100 ms...)
scores.rationale: The interpretation assumption is explicit, latency is labeled an aim rather than fact, and key unknowns (offline requirement, concurrency targets) are surfaced as decisions, though sensitivity analysis is limited.

scores.evidence: Monitoring: sync delay, connection counts and alerts if copies of a document drift apart.
scores.rationale: Crash durability, reconnection, drift detection, rate/size limits and socket permission bypass are concrete, but recovery from detected drift is unspecified and mid-session revocation and client version skew are missing.

scores.evidence: Rate limiting, size limits on documents and updates, and periodic compaction of the stored edit history.
scores.rationale: Domain-meaningful monitoring signals and abuse limits are named, but deployment, rollback, schema/protocol migration and incident ownership are absent.

scores.evidence: That can work in days rather than weeks.
scores.rationale: Beyond a rough demo-effort remark, money, compute, vendor and running costs and their growth with usage are entirely unexamined.

scores.evidence: Choose how edits get merged. This choice shapes everything else.
scores.rationale: The hardest-to-reverse decision (merge model) is correctly identified and front-loaded, but lock-in to the persisted CRDT update format, exit paths and migration strategies are never discussed.

scores.evidence: Shortest path to a demo: steps 1, 4, 7, 8, 11 and 15 with Yjs, TipTap and Hocuspocus.
scores.rationale: Lean, phased design where scaling machinery is deferred to Phase 7 and every component earns its place; slight under-scoping (protocol versioning, collaborative undo) and the partially throwaway Phase 1 REST layer keep it off a 4.

scores.evidence: Milestone: two browser tabs edit the same document live and stay in sync.
scores.rationale: Concrete steps with named libraries, dependency-justified ordering and checkable milestones per phase let a team start immediately; it only lacks explicit contingency if early results disappoint.

checklist.evidence: CRDT (Yjs or Automerge): Recommended. It supports offline editing and peer-to-peer setups, and mature libraries exist.
Choose the document model: plain text, rich text (ProseMirror, TipTap, Lexical, Slate) or block-based.
Write tests that simulate several users making conflicting edits at once and confirm all copies end up the same.
Store CRDT updates on the server, plus periodic snapshots... the server restarts while people are editing, and nothing is lost.
Run multiple WebSocket servers, using Redis pub/sub so they share updates, with each document handled by one server at a time.
Add offline support with a local cache in IndexedDB.
document permissions (owner, editor, commenter, viewer), checked on the WebSocket connection as well as the API.
Version history: named snapshots, comparing versions and restoring.
Show who else is in the document: their cursors, selections, names and colors.
This is the riskiest part of the project, so test it early.
Load testing with many simulated editors on one document.

traps.evidence: Choose how edits get merged. This choice shapes everything else.
Milestone: the server restarts while people are editing, and nothing is lost.

note: A lean, technically sound, correctly sequenced CRDT-based plan with early convergence testing and checkable milestones; its main gaps are protocol/version compatibility, collaborative undo semantics, mid-session permission revocation, deployment/rollback operations, and cost reasoning.
